title: Boston piano styles: stride, ragtime and swing
summary: Whaley and Hinton go through the pianists again, including Skinny Johnson and Walter Johnson, and he says ragtime was swing and every pianist had to stride.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Sure. Well, okay, so you named all these piano players here. Do you think you missed anybody?
Oh, yeah, let me see.
George Rickson we talked about.
George Rickson.
And then there was Joe Burrough and his brother Eubie Burrough. Then we had Dan Curry --
Dan Carey.
Dan Carey, excuse me. Who couldn't read too well, and there was -- what's that guy, Walter Johnson.

Yeah, Walter Johnson. He was the greatest of them all. And there was another fellow named Skinny Johnson. Oh, he was about six feet two or something, and when he played he'd wrap one leg around the other and sit down there. Oh, he could really play.
Now, what type of feeling went into it? Was it jazz or was it --
Ragtime was -- I would call it swing music. That's what they were playing. They were playing swing music. You see, --
Well, did you have to stride like with the left hand or --
Oh, yeah. You wasn't a piano player if you didn't stride.
I see.
And make that left hand go.
Then you had Freddy Turner. You mentioned --
Tunstol.
Tunstol.
Yeah.
He also copied music.
Yeah, yeah. He wrote a number -- what was the name of that? Well, anyway, it became very popular. And I'm trying to think of this other guy.
You mentioned Sabie Lewis. You already told me about Sabie Lewis.
Sabie Lewis, yeah, he was --
And Henry Bachelor.
Henry Bachelor, yeah. Right, they were -- see, they all were --
And Tom Whaley.
